## Introduction to Left Lobe Liver Transplantation

- Living-donor liver transplantation (LDLT) established for end-stage liver disease (ESLD)
- First performed in children (1989) using left lateral segment (LLS)
- Extended to adults (1993) using left lobe (LL) allograft
- Addresses organ shortage crisis with stagnant cadaveric transplantation rates
- Wait-list mortality nearly 25% in United States

## Key Points Overview

- LL LDLT is safe and effective treatment for ESLD
- Shifts risks from donor to recipient
- Small-for-size syndrome (SFSS) previously limited LL use
- Graft inflow modification (GIM) techniques eliminated SFSS risks
- Two clinical forms of GIM: splenic artery ligation/splenectomy and portosystemic shunts
- Long-term outcomes comparable to cadaveric liver transplantation
- Preference for LL LDLT when possible - safer for donor and ethically correct

## Organ Shortage Crisis

- More than 5000 cadaveric liver transplants annually in US
- Stagnant transplantation rates for several years
- Strategies to expand donor pool:
  - Split-liver transplantation
  - Older donors
  - Hemodynamically unstable donors
  - Hepatitis B/C antibody-positive donors
  - Donation after cardiac death (DCD)
- Marginal expansion of donor pool despite these strategies

## LDLT Potential and Limitations

- Great potential to address donor shortage
- Concerns about donor safety limit expansion in Western countries
- Risk of donor morbidity and mortality proportional to:
  - Extent of hepatectomy
  - Remnant liver volume
- Least risk: LLS donation
- Highest risk: Right lobe (RL) donation

## Recipient Considerations

- Graft volume (GV) adequacy most important determinant for success
- Minimum 40% of recipient's standard liver volume (SLV) required
- Early series showed poor outcomes with small grafts:
  - GRWR < 0.8% had 3-month graft survival of only 54.5%
- Small-for-size grafts (SFSGs) caused imbalance between regeneration and function demand

## Small-for-Size Syndrome (SFSS)

- Defined by Dahm and colleagues:
  - GRWR < 0.8%
  - 2+ of following findings on 3 consecutive days within first week:
    - Bilirubin > 10 mg/dL
    - INR > 2.0
    - Encephalopathy grade 3-4
- Multifactorial etiology with portal hyperperfusion as major factor

## Animal Model Findings

- Sinusoidal congestion, rupture, hemorrhage within minutes of reperfusion
- Changes not seen in full liver allografts
- Severity inversely related to allograft size
- Partial diversion of portal flow reduces changes and improves graft function

## Evolution of Graft Selection

- Initially used LL due to familiarity with LLS in pediatric population
- Lower morbidity with LL hepatectomy
- GV often < 40% of recipient's SLV
- Led to inferior short- and long-term outcomes
- RL became allograft of choice despite higher donor risk

## Graft Inflow Modification (GIM)

- Cumulative experience over 2 decades
- Better understanding of SFSS pathophysiology
- Successful application of GIM techniques
- Made graft volume less critical factor
- Small GV (GV/SLV < 40%, GRWR 0.6%) can be successfully used with GIM

## Technical Refinements

- Relatively lower risk of complications with LL LDLT
- Comparable outcomes to cadaveric transplantation
- Overriding concern for donor safety
- LL allograft should be graft of choice whenever possible
- Fundamentally shifts risks from donor to recipient

## Preoperative Planning: 3-Step Process

1. Clinical assessment and serologic testing
2. Radiologic imaging
3. Liver biopsy (optional)

## Donor Eligibility Criteria

- Healthy adults aged 18-60 years
- ABO compatible
- Complete history and physical examination
- BMI calculation
- Laboratory testing:
  - Complete blood count
  - Serum chemistries
  - Thyroid function tests
  - Coagulation profile
  - Viral screening (Hep A/B/C, HIV, EBV, CMV, syphilis)
  - Hypercholesterolemia screening
  - Hypercoagulability workup
  - Diabetes screening

## Donor Screening Requirements

- Mammography, colonoscopy, Papanicolaou smear, PSA up to date
- Antimitochondrial antibody screen for family history of primary biliary cirrhosis
- Psychological/psychiatric evaluation
- No active or uncontrolled psychiatric disorders
- No psychosocial, motivational, or ethical issues
- Smoking cessation for 6 weeks pre-surgery
- Oral contraceptive cessation for female donors
- Cardiac clearance for hypertension or age > 50 years

## Radiologic Assessment

- Delineate liver anatomy:
  - Hepatic veins
  - Portal vein
  - Hepatic artery
  - Biliary system
- Volumetric analysis of individual lobes
- Assessment of hepatic steatosis
- MRI with MRCP preferred modality
- Institutional practices may vary

## Limitations of MRCP

- Spatial resolution often inadequate for intrahepatic biliary anatomy
- Especially problematic with:
  - Small caliber biliary tree
  - Excessive patient movement during testing
- May miss important anatomical variations

## Volumetric Assessment Importance

- Accurate size matching essential
- Ensure adequate functional hepatic mass for recipient
- Sustain metabolic needs
- Permit regeneration
- Avoid SFSS
- GRWR of 0.8% required
- Graft weight to SLV: 30-40%
- Remnant liver volume: 30-40% of original volume

## Specialized Software Tools

- MeVis Liver Analyzer and Liver View
- Produce 3D liver models for volume measurements
- Preoperative planning of surgical planes
- Identify vascular and biliary variations
- Assist in decision-making process

## Volumetric Analysis Accuracy

- Good correlation between actual GVs and radiologically assessed volumes
- Margin of error: 5-25%
- Main cause of discrepancies: graft perfusion
- Imaging measures perfused liver volume
- Weight measurements performed when graft is blood-free

## Comprehensive Road Map Benefits

- Facilitates detailed surgical planning
- Reduces postoperative complications
- For both donor and recipient
- Identifies anatomical variations that may:
  - Affect allograft size
  - Contraindicate hepatectomy

## Hepatic Arterial Anatomy Variations

- Present in nearly 45% of cases
- Variant dominant supply to segment IV by right hepatic artery (11%)
- Significant anomaly for LL transplants
- May require double arterial anastomoses (LHA and segment IV variant artery)
- Separate origins of segment II and III branches from proper hepatic artery
- May require multiple arterial anastomoses

## Hepatic Venous and Portal Venous Anatomy

- Variations less common for LL allografts
- Makes LL allograft technically easier to harvest and implant
- Simpler surgical approach compared to RL

## Biliary Anatomy Variations

- Present in nearly 40% of population
- Critical for LDLT due to high biliary complication rates
- Significant variants include:
  - Common hepatic duct trifurcation
  - Drainage of right hepatic duct system into left duct system
  - Drainage of right posterior duct into left main duct

## Preoperative Liver Biopsy Role

- Controversial role
- Practices vary worldwide
- Vancouver Forum guidelines recommend biopsy for:
  - Abnormal liver function tests
  - Evidence of steatosis
  - Other imaging abnormalities
  - Genetically related donors to recipients with autoimmune hepatitis, PSC, or PBC
  - BMI > 30 kg/m²

## Biopsy Considerations

- Invasive part of donor evaluation
- Potential complications
- Usually performed just before scheduling LDLT
  - Allows ruling out other exclusion criteria

## Voluntary and Informed Consent

- Primary selection criterion for LDLT donation
- Donor must understand risks:
  - Primary nonfunction
  - Recurrence of liver disease in allograft
  - Graft loss from technical reasons or rejection
  - Death of recipient

## Consent Process Details

- Provide information about:
  - Center's LDLT experience
  - Cadaveric LT outcomes
  - Complex hepatobiliary surgeries
  - Short- and long-term donor morbidities, mortality, and outcomes
- Review consent process privately with donor
- Ensure no coercion present

## Donor Rights in Consent Process

- Right to withdraw from process at any time until surgery
- Complete autonomy maintained throughout evaluation
- Ethical imperative for transparent communication

## Anesthesia Management Goals

- Safest anesthetic with minimal morbidity
- Address key issues:
  - Hypothermia prevention
  - Maintenance of low central venous pressure (CVP)
  - Postoperative analgesia

## Anesthesia Risks for Donors

- No more than general anesthesia for complex abdominal surgery
- Standard risk profile comparable to other major surgeries

## Deep Venous Thrombosis Prophylaxis

- Both chemoprophylaxis and mechanical prophylaxis used
- Standard protocol for all donors
- Essential component of perioperative care

## CVP Management During Hepatectomy

- Maintain low levels (0-5 cm)
- Combination approach:
  - Fluid restriction
  - Venodilatory agents if necessary
- Prevent sympathetic stimulation during induction

## Blood Transfusion Policy

- No homologous or autologous blood transfusions for donors
- Cell-saver device used to minimize blood loss
- Storage of autologous blood used by some centers for right liver donation

## Monitoring and Positioning

- Arterial line and 9F central venous catheter for invasive monitoring
- Rapid fluid administration capability
- Hypothermia prevention:
  - Monitor room temperature
  - Active warming with hot-air devices
- Nasogastric tube and Foley catheter placement
- Supine position with right arm extended at 90°, left arm at side

## Antibiotic Prophylaxis

- Administered within 60 minutes before incision
- Per institutional protocol
- Standard surgical prophylaxis

## Donor Hepatectomy: Incision

- Right subcostal incision with left subcostal extension
- 2 finger breadths below costal margin
- Preferred for ease of mobilization of both right and left lobes
- Access to retrohepatic inferior vena cava (IVC)
- Midline extension toward xiphoid process occasionally required
  - For deep abdominal cavity extending high under rib cage

## Alternative Approaches

- Laparoscopic-assisted hepatectomies described
- Completely laparoscopic hepatectomies recently described
- Not currently standard of care

## Initial Surgical Steps

- Bimanual palpation of liver to estimate GV
- Preoperative estimates can occasionally be misleading
- Falciform ligament taken down to insertion at hepatic veins-IVC junction
- Self-retaining retractor system established for exposure

## Intraoperative Ultrasonography (IOUS)

- Review portal and hepatic venous anatomy
- Evaluate for occult lesions missed on preoperative imaging
- Essential diagnostic tool during procedure

## Left Triangular Ligament Division

- Mobilize left lateral segment (LLS)
- Dissection to level of left phrenic vein insertion into left hepatic vein (LHV)
- Medial dissection until medial aspects of LHV and IVC exposed

## Hepatic Vein Exposure

- Confluence of LHV and middle hepatic vein (MHV) exposed
- Low insertions of left phrenic vein and ligamentum venosum divided
- Medial aspect of LHV exposed
- Overlying liver tissue divided if LHV inserts low into IVC

## Hepatoduodenal and Hepatogastric Ligaments

- Exposed by retracting LLS cephalad and distal stomach caudally
- Hepatogastric ligament divided
- Accessory or replaced LHA encountered and preserved
- Aberrant vessels dissected to origin from left gastric artery

## Hepatic Artery Dissection

- Hepatoduodenal ligament opened along medial aspect
- LHA exposed and dissected proximally to origin from hepatic artery proper
- Distally dissected until anterior surface of left portal vein (LPV) exposed
- Proper hepatic artery dissection discouraged to avoid remnant liver injury

## Portal Vein Mobilization

- LHA gently retracted with vessel loop laterally
- Anterior exposure of LPV achieved
- LPV mobilized circumferentially
- Short portal branches to segment IV divided between fine silk ligatures

## Hilar Plate Dissection

- Tissue along medial aspect of hilar plate divided
- Additional retraction of quadrate lobe cephalad
- Helps identify left hepatic duct cephalad to LHA and anterior to LPV

## Biliary Anatomy Dissection

- Confluence of right and left hepatic ducts dissected out
- Care taken not to skeletonize ducts to preserve blood supply
- Prevents biliary complications

## Cholangiogram Preparation

- Large hemoclip placed on periductal tissue at anticipated transection site
- Gallbladder mobilized using fundus-first approach
- Transcystic cholangiogram performed to:
  - Confirm biliary anatomy
  - Identify occult accessory ducts
  - Determine hepatic duct confluence location relative to hemoclip

## Caudate Lobe Mobilization

- Peritoneum divided along left border from hepatic veins to IVC
- Small direct hepatic venous branches from caudate lobe to IVC encountered
- Branches ligated with fine silk ties or divided using tissue-sealing device

## Final IOUS and Transection Planning

- IOUS performed to identify hepatic vein course and branches
- Liver capsule marked with diathermy 1 cm right of MHV course
- Marks anterior projection of parenchymal transection plane
- Extends posteriorly to anterior surface of IVC

## Biliary Transection

- Left hepatic duct sharply transected at level determined by cholangiogram
- Precise anatomical localization critical for success

## Penrose Drain Placement

- Passed posterior to liver, in front of hilar structures inferiorly
- Brought out superiorly anterior to IVC and right of MHV
- Facilitates retraction and exposure

## Parenchymal Transection

- Initiated in gallbladder fossa
- Continued with Cavitron Ultrasonic Surgical Aspirator (CUSA)
- Precise dissection technique essential

## Anticoagulation and Vascular Control

- Patient anticoagulated with 60 U/kg heparin intravenously
- LHA ligated and divided sharply
- Vascular clamp placed on LPV, then divided sharply
- MHV and LHV clamped distal to confluence close to IVC and divided sharply

## Graft Procurement

- Specimen transferred to back table
- Flushed with cold preservative solution
- Transferred to recipient room on ice
- Immediate preservation critical

## Donor Site Closure

- Stumps of hepatic vein and portal vein oversewn with nonabsorbable polypropylene suture
- Left hepatic duct stump oversewn with 6-0 Maxon or PDS suture in running fashion
- Cut surface examined for bleeding and bile leakage
- Small ducts transected during dissection identified and oversewn with 6-0 Maxon suture

## Drain Placement and Abdominal Closure

- Closed-suction drain placed along cut surface of liver
- Abdomen closed in standard 2-layer fashion with heavy absorbable sutures
- Patient extubated in operating room
- Transferred to PACU, then ICU for first 24 hours

## Recipient Hepatectomy: Incision

- Standard right subcostal incision with left extension
- Enter abdominal cavity
- Mobilize liver akin to cadaveric transplantation

## Hilar Dissection

- Right hepatic artery and LHA individually ligated
- Common bile duct divided as high as possible
- Right, left, and main portal veins circumferentially dissected

## Liver Mobilization

- Liver mobilized off retrohepatic IVC
- Right, middle, and left hepatic veins isolated
- Clamps placed across main portal vein and hepatic veins proximal to IVC insertion

## Vascular Division

- Right and left portal veins divided
- Right, middle, and left hepatic veins divided close to liver
- Decision made regarding hemi-portacaval shunt (HPCS) creation based on allograft weight

## GIM Decision Criteria

- GW/RW ratio < 0.8%: routine splenic artery ligation
- Portal venous pressure > 15 mm Hg: HPCS indicated
- Portal venous flow (PVF) > 250 mL/min/100g liver tissue: HPCS indicated
- Simple venting of native portal vein can provide flow estimation

## HPCS Creation

- Right portal vein anastomosed to IVC in end-to-side fashion
- Large hemoclip placed on right portal vein
- Left portal vein prepared for allograft implantation

## Allograft Implantation

- Allograft positioned in subhepatic fossa
- Left hepatic vein anastomosed to recipient's left hepatic vein-IVC confluence
- Running suture technique with nonabsorbable polypropylene

## Portal Vein Anastomosis

- Left portal vein anastomosed to recipient's left portal vein
- Running suture technique with 6-0 or 7-0 polypropylene
- Growth factor left to prevent purse-string effect

## Reperfusion

- Hepatic vein clamp removed first
- Portal vein clamp removed slowly
- Reperfusion of allograft begins
- Hemodynamic monitoring critical during this phase

## Arterial Anastomosis

- Left hepatic artery anastomosed to recipient's left hepatic artery
- Microsurgical technique with 8-0 or 9-0 nylon
- Loupe magnification typically used
- Careful handling to prevent intimal dissection

## Biliary Reconstruction

- Duct-to-duct anastomosis preferred when possible
- Roux-en-Y hepaticojejunostomy if duct-to-duct not feasible
- 6-0 or 7-0 PDS interrupted sutures
- T-tube placement optional

## Completion of Implantation

- Hemostasis verified
- All anastomoses inspected for patency
- Doppler ultrasound performed to confirm vascular flow
- Biliary anastomosis integrity confirmed
- Abdominal closure in layers

## Postoperative Monitoring

- ICU monitoring for first 24-48 hours
- Serial liver function tests
- Doppler ultrasound surveillance
- Coagulation profile monitoring
- Early detection of complications

## Vascular Complications

- Hepatic artery thrombosis: most serious
- Portal vein thrombosis: less common
- Hepatic venous outflow obstruction
- Requires urgent intervention
- May require re-transplantation

## Biliary Complications

- Most common complication after LDLT
- Bile leaks from cut surface or anastomotic site
- Biliary strictures: anastomotic or non-anastomotic
- Management: ERCP, PTC, or surgical revision

## Small-for-Size Syndrome Management

- Early recognition critical
- Supportive care: albumin, diuretics, fresh frozen plasma
- GIM techniques prevent majority of cases
- Plasmapheresis in severe cases
- Re-transplantation as last resort

## Immunosuppression Protocol

- Similar to cadaveric liver transplantation
- Calcineurin inhibitor-based (tacrolimus)
- Steroid taper
- Mycophenolate mofetil
- Individualized based on renal function and complications

## Long-Term Outcomes

- Graft survival comparable to cadaveric transplantation
- Patient survival similar between LL and RL LDLT
- Quality of life excellent for both donors and recipients
- Low recurrence rate of original liver disease

## Donor Outcomes

- Most donors return to normal activity within 3 months
- Low morbidity rate (<10%)
- Mortality rate <0.5%
- Most common complications: wound infection, bile leak, incisional hernia
- Long-term liver function normal

## Advantages of LL LDLT

- Lower donor morbidity compared to RL
- Simpler surgical technique
- Adequate graft volume for many recipients
- GIM techniques overcome size limitations
- Ethically preferable due to donor safety

## Limitations of LL LDLT

- May not provide adequate volume for large recipients
- Technical complexity of GIM techniques
- Requires experienced surgical team
- Not suitable for all recipients

## Future Directions

- Robotic-assisted donor hepatectomy
- Improved imaging techniques
- Better understanding of regeneration
- Bioengineered liver grafts
- Xenotransplantation developments

## Ethical Considerations

- Donor safety paramount
- Informed consent process
- Risk-benefit analysis for both donor and recipient
- Equitable organ allocation
- Transparency in outcomes reporting

## Conclusion

- LL LDLT is safe and effective for ESLD
- GIM techniques have revolutionized the field
- Outcomes comparable to cadaveric transplantation
- Donor safety is primary consideration
- Should be preferred over RL LDLT when feasible
- Continued refinement will improve outcomes further

## Key Takeaways

- LL LDLT shifts risk from donor to recipient
- GIM techniques eliminate SFSS concerns
- Long-term outcomes excellent
- Donor morbidity low with LL approach
- Multidisciplinary team essential for success
- Patient selection critical for optimal outcomes

## Clinical Pearls

- Always confirm anatomy with cholangiogram
- Maintain low CVP during donor hepatectomy
- Use growth factor in vascular anastomoses
- Monitor portal pressure during reperfusion
- Early detection of complications crucial

## Technical Tips

- CUSA settings: 70-80% amplitude, 70-80% irrigation
- Suture selection: 6-0 PDS for biliary, 5-0/6-0 for vascular
- Drain placement: near biliary anastomosis
- Retractor positioning: adequate exposure essential

## Pearls for Residents

- Understand hepatic segmental anatomy
- Practice microsurgical techniques
- Learn to interpret intraoperative ultrasound
- Recognize anatomical variations early
- Communicate effectively with team
